stem: What does Twain mean when he writes that in Virginia City "speculation ran riot, and yet there was a world of substantial business going on, too"?

stimulus.source_note: Mark Twain, Roughing It (1872), ch. 52. Public domain. Text verified against the Standard Ebooks edition (standardebooks.org/ebooks/mark-twain/roughing-it/text/chapter-52).
stimulus.text:
Mark Twain, Roughing It (1872), Chapter 52, on Virginia City, Nevada:

"The year 1863 was perhaps the very top blossom and culmination of the 'flush times.' Virginia swarmed with men and vehicles to that degree that the place looked like a very hive—that is when one's vision could pierce through the thick fog of alkali dust that was generally blowing in summer... Speculation ran riot, and yet there was a world of substantial business going on, too. All freights were brought over the mountains from California (150 miles) by pack-train partly, and partly in huge wagons drawn by such long mule teams that each team amounted to a procession... All the bullion was shipped in bars by stage to San Francisco... There were three stages a day, each way, and I have seen the out-going stages carry away a third of a ton of bullion each, and more than once I saw them divide a two-ton lot and take it off."

"All along under the center of Virginia and Gold Hill, for a couple of miles, ran the great Comstock silver lode — a vein of ore from fifty to eighty feet thick between its solid walls of rock — a vein as wide as some of New York's streets."

"Virginia was a busy city of streets and houses above ground. Under it was another busy city, down in the bowels of the earth, where a great population of men thronged in and out among an intricate maze of tunnels and drifts, flitting hither and thither under a winking sparkle of lights, and over their heads towered a vast web of interlocking timbers that held the walls of the gutted Comstock apart."

options.text: The town's economy was entirely fake, with no real mining at all
options.misconception: Background: Twain describes a real underground city of tunnels and timbers; the silver was real and the mining was large-scale.

options.text: Wild gambling on mining shares went on alongside genuine, large-scale silver mining
The townspeople had stopped mining and lived only by trading stocks
options.misconception: Background: the tunnels, drifts, and timbering Twain describes are working mines, not abandoned holes.

options.text: The federal government had banned all private mining in Nevada
options.misconception: Background: mining in Nevada was private enterprise; the government never banned it, and the Comstock mines made fortunes.

rationales.A: Background: the lode was real, fifty to eighty feet thick, and the underground city of tunnels was a working mine. The business was substantial, not fake.
rationales.B: Twain holds both halves at once: the 'flush times' frenzy of speculation, and beneath it a real industry of shafts, tunnels, and bullion shipped by stage.
rationales.C: Background: the men thronging the tunnels are miners at work. Trading shares happened above ground; digging happened below it.
rationales.D: Background: the Comstock mines were private ventures. No federal ban existed, and the mines poured out silver for decades.
rationales.general:
Twain is holding two pictures at once: the casino upstairs and the mine below.
1. Take the first half: speculation ran riot in the flush times.
2. Take the second half: a world of substantial business, tunnels, timbers, and bullion bars shipped to San Francisco.
3. Put them together. A boomtown gambles on top of real work, and both are the story.
Remember: in a boom, the betting and the business grow together, so do not mistake one for the other.
